title: The Disappearance of William Morgan
bigQuestion: How did one man's disappearance in 1826 change the way Americans felt about secret societies and politics?

story.title: A Carriage in the Dark
story.kicker: On a September night in 1826, a man walks out of a small-town jail in New York and is never seen again.
paragraphs: It is the night of September 12, 1826. The town of Canandaigua, in western New York, is dark and quiet. Inside the county jail sits a man named William Morgan. He is there because he owes a small debt to an innkeeper, less than three dollars. The day before, he was at home in the town of Batavia, about fifty miles to the west.

Morgan has made some people very angry. He has been working on a book. It promises to print the secret ceremonies of the Freemasons, a brotherhood with lodges in almost every town. Many Masons feel he is breaking a solemn promise. Some of them are furious.

That night, men come to the jail and pay what Morgan owes. He is let out into the dark. Witnesses later say he struggled and called for help. He is put into a waiting carriage. The carriage rolls west toward Fort Niagara, where the Niagara River separates New York from Canada.

William Morgan was never seen again. No one has ever proved what happened to him. But his disappearance set off a storm. Within a few years, hundreds of Masonic lodges closed. A new political party was born. Even the way Americans choose candidates for president changed.
story.think: Why might a mystery with no clear answer make people angrier than a crime that is solved in court?

lessons.title: Morgan's Book Plan
lessons.mainIdea: In 1826 William Morgan of Batavia, New York, planned to publish a book revealing Masonic rituals, and that plan put him in danger.
reading: Batavia was a small town in western New York in 1826. The Erie Canal had opened the year before, and towns across the region were growing fast. William Morgan lived in Batavia with his wife and young children. He had taken part in Masonic lodge meetings. Now he had a different plan.

Morgan teamed up with a Batavia printer named David C. Miller. Together they planned a book called Illustrations of Masonry. On August 14, 1826, the title was filed for copyright. The book promised to print the secret words, signs and ceremonies that Masons used in their lodges.

A book like this is called an *exposé*. An exposé reveals something a group wanted kept hidden. Exposés of Masonry were not new. One had been printed in London almost a hundred years earlier. But in a small town where everyone knew each other, this one felt personal.

Each Masonic ceremony followed a *ritual*. A ritual is a set of words and actions done the same way each time. For Masons, rituals marked each step a member took in the brotherhood. Many members felt that printing them was a betrayal.

words.d: a piece of writing that reveals something a group wanted kept hidden
a set of words and actions done the same way each time, often in a ceremony

look.title: A Printer's Shop in Batavia
look.text: Picture a small printing shop in 1826. Sheets of damp paper hang drying on a line. A printer sets tiny metal letters, one by one, into a frame. A man beside him reads aloud from handwritten pages about passwords and handshakes. Both men know that many of their neighbors will be angry when the book comes out.
look.prompt: Why might a writer and a printer take this risk? List one reason they might have had and one danger they faced.

check.q: What did William Morgan plan to publish in 1826?
choices: A map of the Erie Canal
A newspaper for a new political party
check.why: The reading says Morgan planned Illustrations of Masonry, which promised to print the Masons' secret words, signs and ceremonies.

check.q: What is an exposé?
choices: A secret handshake used in a lodge
A promise made in a ceremony
A piece of writing that reveals what a group wanted hidden
A court order to free a prisoner
check.why: An exposé reveals something a group wanted kept hidden, as Morgan's book tried to do.

check.q: Who worked with Morgan on the book?
check.why: The reading says Morgan teamed up with David C. Miller, a printer in Batavia.

lessons.title: Promises Inside the Lodge
lessons.mainIdea: Masons saw their secret signs and promises as a sign of trust, while critics saw secret oaths as a danger to fair government.
reading: Imagine joining a club where members help each other's families when times are hard. To join, you make a serious promise to keep the club's words and signs private. In the 1820s, many thousands of American men belonged to clubs like this. The best known was the Freemasons.

Masons met in a *lodge*. The word means both the local group and the room where it meets. Members were farmers, shopkeepers, lawyers and judges. They said the lodge taught good character and charity. They said the secret signs helped them trust a brother Mason from another town.

To join, a man took an *oath*. An oath is a solemn promise, often made before God. Masonic oaths promised to keep the lodge's secrets. Some oaths named harsh penalties for breaking the promise. Masons said these penalties were symbols of how serious the promise was.

Critics saw the same oaths differently. They asked: what if a Mason's promise to his lodge came before his duty to the law? What if a judge or a juror favored a brother Mason? After Morgan vanished, that question swept across the country.

words.d: a local group of Masons, and also the room where they meet
a solemn promise, often made before God

look.title: Two Ways to See One Promise
look.text: A lodge member says: My oath means my brothers can trust me, and I will help their widows and children. A critic says: A secret oath could make a man protect his brothers even when they break the law. Both speakers are talking about the very same promise.
look.prompt: What does each speaker care about most? What facts would you want before deciding which view fits a real case?

check.q: What is an oath?
choices: A secret password for a meeting
A room where a club meets
A book that reveals a club's secrets
A solemn promise, often made before God
check.why: The reading defines an oath as a solemn promise, often made before God. Masons took one when they joined.

check.q: According to the reading, why did Masons say their secret signs were useful?
choices: They helped members trust a brother Mason from another town
They were needed to enter churches
They let members skip paying debts
check.why: Masons said the signs helped them trust a brother Mason from another town.

check.q: What worry did critics have about Masonic oaths?
choices: That the oaths were written in Latin
That a Mason might favor his lodge brothers over the law
That the oaths cost too much money
That children had to take the oaths too
check.why: Critics asked whether a Mason's promise to his lodge might come before his duty to the law.

lessons.title: Arrested and Jailed
lessons.mainIdea: Morgan was arrested on September 11, 1826, on a small theft charge that was dropped, and then he was held in the Canandaigua jail for a tiny debt.
reading: On September 11, 1826, officers arrested William Morgan. The *charge* was petty theft, over a shirt and a tie. A charge is a formal claim that a person broke the law. A charge is not proof. It still has to be shown in court.

Morgan was taken about fifty miles east to the jail at Canandaigua. There the theft charge was dropped. For a moment he was free. Then he was arrested again. This time it was for a *debt* of about $2.69 that he owed an innkeeper.

Why does this matter? A debt of less than three dollars was a small sum, even in 1826. Many people later believed the charges were a trick. They thought someone wanted Morgan locked up far from home, away from his friends and his printer.

The arrests themselves are well recorded. Whether they were planned as a trap is a harder question. It fits what happened next. People who study the case still weigh how much was planned ahead, and by whom.

words.d: a formal claim that a person broke the law; it is not proof
money that a person owes to someone else

look.title: Two Days in Order
look.text: September 11: Morgan is arrested for petty theft. He is taken to Canandaigua. The theft charge is dropped. He is jailed again for a debt of about $2.69. September 12, at night: men pay the debt, and Morgan walks out of the jail.
look.prompt: Look at the order of events. Which step seems most surprising to you? Why might people have become suspicious?

check.q: Where was Morgan held after his arrest?
check.why: The reading says Morgan was taken about fifty miles east to the jail at Canandaigua.

check.q: What happened to the theft charge?
choices: It led to a two-year sentence
It was proven by a jury
check.why: At Canandaigua the theft charge was dropped, and Morgan was then jailed for a small debt.

check.q: Why did many people think the arrests were a trick?
choices: Morgan had never been to Batavia
The charges were small and kept him far from home
check.why: The charges were tiny, and they kept Morgan locked up far from his friends and his printer.

lessons.title: Taken in the Night
lessons.mainIdea: On the night of September 12, 1826, men paid Morgan's debt and took him from the jail by carriage toward Fort Niagara, and he was never seen again.
reading: On the night of September 12, a group of men came to the Canandaigua jail. They paid Morgan's small debt, so the jail let him go. Outside, he was put into a carriage. Witnesses later said he struggled and called for help.

Taking a person away by force is called *abduction*. The carriage traveled west across New York. Its goal was Fort Niagara, an old fort where the Niagara River flows into Lake Ontario. Canada lies just across the river.
Reports later said Morgan was held at the fort for a short time. After that, the trail goes cold. No one has ever produced a confirmed record of where he went or what happened to him.

Several parts of that night are *documented*, which means written records support them. The arrest, the jail, the paid debt and the carriage ride are all documented. His fate is not. That gap between the known and the unknown is where rumors grew.

words.d: taking a person away by force
supported by written records or other solid evidence

look.title: A Route Across New York
look.text: Trace a line on a map of New York. Start at Batavia. Move east to Canandaigua and its jail. Then turn and travel far west, past Batavia again, to Fort Niagara. There the Niagara River flows into Lake Ontario, and Canada lies just across the water.
look.prompt: Why might the men have chosen a place on the border with Canada? What does the route suggest, and what does it not prove?

check.q: What is an abduction?
choices: Paying off a debt for someone
Choosing a candidate at a meeting
Taking a person away by force
check.why: The reading defines abduction as taking a person away by force, as happened to Morgan.

check.q: Where was the carriage headed?
choices: Fort Niagara, on the border with Canada
check.why: The carriage went west toward Fort Niagara, where the Niagara River meets Lake Ontario across from Canada.

check.q: Which part of the story is NOT documented?
choices: The paid debt at the jail
The carriage ride from the jail
check.why: The reading says the arrest, jail, debt and carriage ride are documented, but his fate is not.

lessons.title: What Happened to Morgan?
lessons.mainIdea: No one has ever proved what happened to Morgan; people offered several theories, and the evidence does not settle them.
reading: Soon after Morgan vanished, people started to guess. Some said he was drowned in the Niagara River. Others said he was paid to leave the country and start a new life. Over the years, stories claimed he had been seen alive in faraway places.

Each guess is a *theory*, an idea that tries to explain what happened. A strong theory fits the evidence. A weak theory asks you to ignore some facts or to trust a rumor. A *rumor* is a story passed from person to person without proof.

The strongest evidence shows that Morgan was taken against his will by men linked to local lodges. It does not show what happened after Fort Niagara. No body was ever confirmed as his. No court ever found anyone guilty of killing him.
Many people believed, then and now, that he was killed. Many Masons argued that a few angry men had done the crime, not the whole order. Historians still treat his fate as an open question.

words.d: an idea that tries to explain what happened
a story passed from person to person without proof

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: Claim A: Men took Morgan from the Canandaigua jail by carriage. Claim B: Morgan was drowned in the Niagara River. Claim C: Morgan was paid to move far away. Claim D: Some of the men who took part were tried in court.
look.prompt: Sort each claim into two piles, documented or unproven. What kind of evidence would move a claim from one pile to the other?

check.q: What is a theory?
choices: A story passed along with no proof
An idea that tries to explain what happened
check.why: A theory is an idea that tries to explain what happened. People had several theories about Morgan.

check.q: According to the reading, what did no court ever do?
choices: Find anyone guilty of killing Morgan
Hold any trial about the case
check.why: The reading says no court ever found anyone guilty of killing Morgan.

check.q: Which statement fits the evidence best?
choices: Morgan was proven to have drowned
Morgan was taken against his will, and his fate is unknown
Morgan's body was buried in Batavia
check.why: The evidence shows he was taken against his will, but it does not show what happened next.

lessons.title: A Body at Oak Orchard Creek
lessons.mainIdea: In 1827 a body was claimed to be Morgan's, but a widow said it was her husband, which shows how people can bend evidence to fit what they want.
reading: In October 1827, more than a year after Morgan vanished, a body was found near Oak Orchard Creek, by Lake Ontario. People who blamed the Masons quickly said it was Morgan. At last, they said, here was proof of murder.
Then a widow came forward. She said the body was her husband, Timothy Munroe, who had drowned. In the end, the body was named as Munroe, not Morgan. The proof that people had hoped for was gone.

A newspaper editor named Thurlow Weed was a leader of the *Anti-Masons*, people who opposed the Masonic order. His critics said he used the body to win votes. Two versions of what Weed said about the body survive, and they paint him very differently.

This is a lesson about *evidence*, the facts that help show whether a claim is true. When people badly want a story to be true, they may grab any clue that seems to fit. A careful reader asks: who is making the claim, what do they gain, and what does other evidence show?

words.d: people who opposed the Masonic order, especially after the Morgan affair
facts or objects that help show whether a claim is true

look.title: Two Versions of One Remark
look.text: The popular version: Weed said the body was a good enough Morgan until after the election. Weed's own version: when told it was not Morgan, he said it was good enough for them until the Masons brought back the man they had carried off.
look.cite: Popular accounts of the Morgan affair, and Thurlow Weed's own account in his autobiography, published 1883 (both paraphrased)
look.prompt: How does each version make Weed look? Why might Weed's own account and his critics' account be different?

check.q: Who did the widow say the body was?
check.why: The widow said the body was her husband, Timothy Munroe, and it was named as Munroe.

check.q: Who were the Anti-Masons?
choices: A group of printers in Batavia
People who opposed the Masonic order
check.why: The reading defines Anti-Masons as people who opposed the Masonic order.

check.q: Why does the reading call the body story a lesson about evidence?
choices: It shows people may grab a clue that fits what they want to believe
It shows newspapers never make mistakes
It proves Weed was a Mason
check.why: People who wanted proof of murder claimed the body too quickly, before the evidence was weighed.

lessons.title: Trials and Short Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: Several men were convicted of kidnapping Morgan, but their sentences ranged only from one month to 28 months.
reading: In January 1827, a court at Canandaigua tried four men named Lawson, Chesebro, Sawyer and Sheldon for their part in taking Morgan. All four were *convicted*, which means found guilty. The crime was *kidnapping*, taking and holding a person by force. Without a body, no one could prove Morgan was dead.

Their sentences were short. A *sentence* is the punishment a court gives. Lawson got two years. Chesebro got one year. Sheldon got three months. Sawyer got one month. None of them was sent away for long.

Later, Eli Bruce, the sheriff of Niagara County, was also convicted. He served 28 months in the Canandaigua jail. New York's governor, DeWitt Clinton, removed him from office. Other men were tried in the years that followed.
To many people, the punishments seemed far too small. A man had vanished, and the longest sentence was just over two years. That feeling of unfairness turned shock into public anger.

words.d: found guilty of a crime by a court
taking and holding a person by force
the punishment a court gives to a person found guilty

look.title: Sentences in the Morgan Kidnapping Cases
look.cite: Court results of 1827-1828 as given in Charles F. Milliken, A History of Ontario County, New York, and Its People (1911), and The Masonic Martyr, a biography of Eli Bruce
look.prompt: How many times longer was the sheriff's sentence than Sawyer's? Why might people expect a public official to be punished more?

check.q: What does convicted mean?
check.why: Convicted means found guilty of a crime by a court, as the four men were in 1827.

check.q: What was the longest sentence in the Morgan cases?
choices: 28 months, served by Sheriff Eli Bruce
check.why: Sheriff Eli Bruce served 28 months, which was longer than Lawson's two years.

check.q: Why were the men charged with kidnapping, not murder?
choices: Without a body, no one could prove Morgan was dead
Murder was not a crime in 1827
Morgan asked the court to go easy
check.why: The reading says that without a body, no one could prove Morgan was dead.

lessons.title: Why the Public Grew Angry
lessons.mainIdea: People grew angry because they suspected Masons in public office had protected each other, even though most Masons had no part in the crime.
reading: Picture a farmer in western New York in 1828. He hears that a man was taken from a jail. He hears that a sheriff helped. He hears that the punishments were small. He starts to wonder who else knew. Many of his neighbors wonder too.

Critics pointed to a pattern. Some officials in the Morgan cases were Masons. Some trials ended with men *acquitted*, or found not guilty. To critics, this looked like a *cover-up*, an effort to hide the truth and protect the guilty.

Masons answered that a small group of men had done the crime. Most Masons had nothing to do with it. They pointed out that Governor Clinton, himself a well-known Mason, removed the sheriff who took part.

Both sides had a point. There was a real crime and there were real reasons for doubt. There was also real unfairness in blaming every member for what a few had done. When a group is secret, it is hard for its members to show outsiders they are innocent. That made the anger last.

words.d: found not guilty by a court
an effort to hide the truth and protect the people responsible

look.title: Two Imagined Letters to the Editor
look.text: Letter 1: A sheriff helped take a man from a jail, and the punishments were tiny. Masons in office protect their own. Letter 2: I am a Mason and a farmer. I never heard of this plot until I read the paper. Why am I treated like a criminal?
look.prompt: Which facts from the lesson support each letter? What would be a fair way to answer both writers?

check.q: What is a cover-up?
choices: An effort to hide the truth
check.why: A cover-up is an effort to hide the truth. Critics believed officials were hiding what happened to Morgan.

check.q: What did critics point to as signs of a cover-up?
choices: Some officials were Masons, and some trials ended with men acquitted
check.why: The reading says critics noted that some officials were Masons and some trials ended in acquittals.

check.q: Why was it hard for ordinary Masons to show they were innocent?
choices: Their group was secret, so outsiders could not see what they did
check.why: The reading says that when a group is secret, it is hard for members to show outsiders they are innocent.

lessons.title: The Anti-Masonic Party
lessons.mainIdea: Anger over the Morgan case grew into the Anti-Masonic Party, often called the first third party in American history.
reading: In February 1828, Thurlow Weed and Samuel Heron started a newspaper in Rochester, New York. It was called the Anti-Masonic Enquirer. Papers like it told the Morgan story again and again. They helped turn local anger into a political movement.

A *political party* is a group that works to elect its members to office. In those years, most voters chose one of two big parties. The Anti-Masons became a *third party*, a party outside the two main ones. It is often called the first third party in American history.

The party was strongest in New York, Vermont and other northeastern states. Its members wanted Masons kept out of public office. They believed secret oaths did not belong in a free country where the people rule.

Well-known people joined the cause. Former president John Quincy Adams wrote public letters against Masonic oaths from 1831 to 1833. They were later collected in a book, Letters on the Masonic Institution, printed in 1847.

words.d: a group that works to elect its members to public office
a political party outside the two main parties

look.title: A Former President Speaks Out
look.text: Adams argued that the Masonic oaths, with their frightening penalties, were wrong. He said such oaths had no place in a free republic. He called on Masons to give them up.
look.cite: John Quincy Adams, Letters on the Masonic Institution (Boston: T. R. Marvin, 1847), letters written 1831-1833 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What does Adams want Masons to change? Why would a former president's words carry extra weight?

check.q: What is a third party?
choices: A party held after an election
A political party outside the two main ones
check.why: A third party is a political party outside the two main ones, like the Anti-Masonic Party.

check.q: Who started the Anti-Masonic Enquirer in Rochester?
choices: William Morgan and David C. Miller
John Quincy Adams and William Wirt
check.why: The reading says Thurlow Weed and Samuel Heron started the paper in February 1828.

check.q: What did the Anti-Masons want?
choices: A new canal to Fort Niagara
Masons kept out of public office
check.why: Anti-Masons wanted Masons kept out of public office because they distrusted secret oaths.

lessons.title: The First National Convention
lessons.mainIdea: In 1831 the Anti-Masons held the first national nominating convention, a way of choosing candidates that parties still use.
reading: Today, every four years, the big parties hold national conventions. Crowds cheer. Delegates from every state choose the party's candidate for president. That custom started with the Anti-Masons.

From September 26 to 28, 1831, about 110 *delegates* from 13 states met in Baltimore, Maryland. A delegate is a person sent to speak and vote for others. It was the first national *nominating convention*, a meeting where a party picks its candidate. Before this, small groups of leaders in Congress often chose candidates.

The delegates chose William Wirt for president. Wirt was a lawyer who had served as U.S. attorney general. Surprisingly, he had once been a Mason himself. The convention also issued an Address to the People. Many historians count it as an early party *platform*, a public list of a party's beliefs and plans.

Other parties soon copied the idea and held national conventions of their own. In the 1832 election, Wirt won only one state, Vermont, with its 7 electoral votes. The party lost, but its way of choosing candidates lasted.

words.d: people sent to speak and vote for a larger group
a meeting where a political party picks its candidate
a public list of a political party's beliefs and plans

look.title: The 1832 Presidential Election
look.cite: Electoral vote totals, 1832 presidential election (U.S. National Archives, Electoral College records)
look.prompt: How many electoral votes did Wirt win? Why might a party that won so few votes still matter in history?

check.q: What happens at a nominating convention?
check.why: A nominating convention is a meeting where a party picks its candidate, as the Anti-Masons did in 1831.

check.q: Where and when did the first national nominating convention meet?
check.why: The Anti-Masons met in Baltimore from September 26 to 28, 1831.

check.q: What surprising fact about William Wirt does the reading give?
choices: He had once been a Mason
check.why: The reading says the Anti-Masonic candidate had once been a Mason himself.

lessons.title: Lodges Close Their Doors
lessons.mainIdea: After the Morgan affair, hundreds of Masonic lodges closed, especially in New York and Vermont.
reading: Anti-Masonic anger hit lodges hard. Some neighbors stopped speaking to members. Churches and families argued about the lodge. Many men quietly quit. Others kept their membership but stopped meeting.

New York had about 480 lodges in 1826. By the 1830s, only about 75 were still working, by common counts. Sources give different numbers, so historians use the word 'about.' Every lodge in Vermont gave up its *charter*, the official paper that lets a lodge meet. In Kentucky, lodges fell from 66 to 37.

The wave reached Illinois too. The first Grand Lodge of Illinois, formed in 1823, stopped meeting around 1827. It was formed again at Jacksonville in 1840. The Panic of 1837, a money crisis, also made it hard for clubs to survive in these years.

The Anti-Masonic Party faded in the later 1830s. Many of its members joined the new Whig Party. Masonry slowly recovered and grew large again later in the century. Its sharp *decline* after 1826 shows how fast public trust can be lost.

words.d: the official paper that gives a lodge or group the right to meet
a drop in size, strength or numbers

look.title: Lodges Before and After the Anti-Masonic Wave
look.cite: Universal Freemasonry, 'Effects of Anti-Masonry on the Fraternity'; common counts, which vary by source
look.prompt: About what share of New York's lodges were still working? Which state lost a larger share, New York or Kentucky?

check.q: What is a lodge charter?
choices: The official paper that lets a lodge meet
check.why: A charter is the official paper that lets a lodge meet. Every Vermont lodge gave its charter up.

check.q: About how many New York lodges were still working in the 1830s, by common counts?
check.why: The reading says New York fell from about 480 lodges to about 75.

check.q: Besides Anti-Masonry, what made it hard for clubs to survive in the late 1830s?
check.why: The reading names the Panic of 1837, a money crisis, as another reason clubs struggled.

lessons.title: Proven and Never Proven
lessons.mainIdea: The Morgan affair shows the difference between what records prove, a kidnapping, and what was never proven, a murder.
reading: In September 1882, a stone monument to William Morgan was dedicated in the cemetery at Batavia. The National Christian Association, a group against secret societies, paid for it. Its words say, as a fact, that Masons murdered him.

A *monument* is a lasting marker that honors a person or event. Monuments can also make a *claim*, a statement that something is true. This monument states something no court ever proved. It tells us what its builders believed 56 years after Morgan vanished.

Here is what records do prove. Morgan was arrested, jailed and taken away by force. Men connected to local lodges were convicted of kidnapping. A national party grew out of the anger. Hundreds of lodges closed.

Here is what was never proven: that Morgan was killed, who killed him, or that the Masonic order as a whole planned it. Keeping these two lists apart is a skill. You can use it every time you read a strong claim about a secret group.

words.d: a lasting marker, often of stone, that honors a person or event
a statement that something is true, which may or may not be proven

look.title: The Words on the Morgan Monument
look.text: The inscription says that Morgan was abducted near this spot in 1826 by Freemasons and murdered for revealing the secrets of their order.
look.cite: Morgan Monument, Batavia Cemetery, Batavia, New York, dedicated 1882 (inscription, paraphrased)
look.prompt: Which part of the inscription matches the court records? Which part goes beyond what any court proved?

check.q: Who paid for the 1882 Morgan Monument?
choices: The Grand Lodge of New York
The National Christian Association, a group against secret societies
check.why: The reading says the National Christian Association paid for the monument.

check.q: Which statement was proven in court?
choices: The Masonic order planned a murder
Morgan drowned in the Niagara River
Men were guilty of kidnapping Morgan
check.why: Courts convicted men of kidnapping. No court proved murder or a plan by the whole order.

check.q: What is a claim?
choices: A statement that something is true, which may or may not be proven
check.why: A claim is a statement that something is true. The monument makes a claim that no court proved.

review.q: Where did William Morgan live when he planned his book?
review.why: Morgan lived in Batavia, New York, where he worked with the printer David C. Miller.

review.q: Which of these events came first?
review.why: Morgan's arrest in September 1826 came before the 1827 trials, the 1831 convention and the 1882 monument.

review.q: Why did Morgan's book plan anger many Masons?
choices: It would print rituals they had promised to keep private
It called for a new party
review.why: Masons had sworn oaths to keep their rituals private, and the book would print them.

review.q: How did the Morgan case change American elections?
choices: It ended the use of paper ballots
It led to the first national nominating convention
It created the office of sheriff
review.why: The Anti-Masonic Party held the first national nominating convention in Baltimore in 1831.

review.q: Which statement best describes Morgan's fate?
choices: He was proven to have drowned
review.why: No body was confirmed and no court found anyone guilty of killing him, so his fate is unknown.

review.q: How is Thurlow Weed connected to the body at Oak Orchard Creek?
choices: Weed said the body was his cousin
Weed was tried for the man's death
Weed built a monument over it
Critics said Weed used the body to win votes
review.why: Weed was an Anti-Masonic editor, and his critics accused him of using the body for politics.

review.q: What did Anti-Masons believe about secret oaths?
choices: They were needed to protect judges
They did not belong in a free country
They should be printed in every newspaper
review.why: Anti-Masons believed secret oaths did not belong in a free country where the people rule.

review.q: Which fact shows the Morgan affair's effect on lodges?
choices: Every Vermont lodge gave up its charter, and New York fell to about 75 lodges
review.why: The reading on lodges says every Vermont lodge gave up its charter and New York fell from about 480 to about 75.
